rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2.1-2.3 - cross-sectional household survey of 383 farmers (195 MI kit users, 187 controls) in four Tanzanian districts, Feb-Mar 2021, with gross margin, partial budgeting and regression analyses plus qualitative interviews. Q2: Sections 3.2.2-3.2.5, Table 3, Figures 3-8 - MI (drip kit) farmers had higher yields, revenue and gross margins for nearly all vegetables; Section 3.3/Table 4 and 3.7 - poverty indicators not significantly different overall; qualitative interviews - half of MI farmers used extra income for schooling. Q4: Figures 3-8 and Table 3 - yield, revenue, variable cost and gross margin per bed measured as the pathway from kits to income/livelihood. Q5: Tables 1-2, 8, A1-A4, Figures 3-8 - results reported separately for Babati (Manyara), Hai (Kilimanjaro), Kasulu (Kigoma) and Kilosa (Morogoro) districts and for several crops. Q6: Tables 4, 7, 8, A1-A4 - household-level poverty/food-security outcomes aggregated at district and multi-district level for a sample drawn from 3444 registered farmers. Q7: Section 3.2.4 and Conclusions - authors state from their results that a higher unit price/market linkages are vital for the gross margin gains and that MI is more effective when combined with market-link initiatives; Section 3.7 - nutrient-deficient soils may not sustain high yields. Q8: Section 4 and 3.4 - cross-sectional snapshot design, no baseline poverty data, possible spillover to control farmers, income-to-poverty translation may take time, soil analysis absent. Q9: Tables 2, 4-6, 8 report means with SD; Figures 3-8 show standard error bars for yield, price, revenue, TVC and GM.
rows.notes: The row function is labelled social_cohesion but the passage claims enhanced livelihoods; the study does not measure social cohesion at all, so the rating follows the passage (livelihoods). Support is mixed: own gross margin/partial budgeting data show higher income for MI farmers, but multivariate analysis found no significant overall association between MI participation and poverty indicators, and in Kasulu MI was associated with more negative coping strategies. The intervention is a bundled kit (drip system plus seeds, fertiliser, pesticides and technical advice), so the effect cannot be attributed to drip alone; controls also reportedly adopted the same techniques. Q3 rated no because quantitative questionnaire and qualitative interviews are both farmer self-report rather than independent measurement methods (doubt noted).

notes: Full text appears complete (abstract through appendix tables and references); some pages contain duplicated/overlapping text from the layout but all results sections are readable.
